\caption{(a) Relative count error $(\hat c-k)/k$ against requested repetitions

\subsection{Models undercount repetitions, proportionally}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(a) shows the relative count error against $k$. Below
$k\!=\!6$ every model is essentially exact; above it, repeated items are rendered
with a median error of \ErrRepCk{}\% per checkpoint, or \ErrRep{}\%
$[\ErrRepLo{},\ErrRepHi{}]$ pooling items ($n=\ErrRepN{}$) --- pooling weights
checkpoints by surviving item count, so we quote both. Either way it is
one-directional: models produce \emph{fewer} repetitions than requested.

Within $k\le32$ that deficit is \emph{proportional}, not saturating --- not what
Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(iv) predicts. The panel's median count above
$k\!=\!6$ is fitted far better by $\hat c=\ShapePropSlope{}k$ than by any
constant (residual sums of squares \ShapePropSSE{} against \ShapeSatSSE{}, S10),
so no horizon lies inside this ladder.

\subsection{Past the ladder, the count does level off}

So we extended it, post hoc (S16 dates every analysis decision against the
commit log), to $k\in\{48,64,96,128\}$ on the \HzNModels{}
checkpoints admitting utterances that long (\HzModelNames{}; XTTS-v2's
$602$-mel-token ceiling censors every $k\ge48$ item, S10). Tracking stops: the
repeated median sits at \HzMedRepKLo{} and \HzMedRepKHi{} at $k\!=\!48$ and
$128$ as the control climbs \HzMedCtlKLo{} to \HzMedCtlKHi{}. Of \HzNGen{} generations \HzExclCap{} hit our
budget and \HzExclDegen{} were degenerate, leaving \HzNCellLo{}--\HzNCellHi{}
per cell; dropping truncated items is conservative, their counts being censored
downward.

The controls stop us reading this as counting collapse alone: they saturate too,
so these decoders have a general utterance-length ceiling and the reportable
quantity is the \emph{ratio}, which divides it out. Fitting $\hat c(k)=\hat
K(1-e^{-k/\hat K})$ over the combined ladder --- $\hat K$ a saturation scale read
off counts, \emph{not} the theorem's $N^\ast$, a function of the unmeasured $q$
--- gives $\hat K_{\mathrm{rep}}=\HzNRep{}$ against
$\hat K_{\mathrm{ctl}}=\HzNCtl{}$ $[\HzNCtlLo{},\HzNCtlHi{}]$: repetition lowers
the counting horizon \HzRatio{}-fold, just past where our ladder stopped, which
is why $k\le32$ looked proportional.

The panel is not unanimous: intervals are disjoint for \HzSepNames{}, while
\HzRevNames{} shows \emph{no} repeated-side saturation within $k\le128$, inverts
the ratio, and is also the checkpoint with no deficit at $k\le32$. Whether its
per-repetition map fails to contract or the effect is absent for some other
reason we cannot say, and we report it as an unexplained exception rather than as
evidence of the theorem behaving conditionally.

The checkpoint, not the generation, is the unit of replication. The exactly-correct rate favours the control in all \CkExactN{} (mean
\CkExact{} points $[\CkExactLo{},\CkExactHi{}]$); the median-error gap is
positive in \CkErrNPos{} of \CkErrN{}, zero in \ErrBestModel{}. Those six
cluster into \FamExactN{} families, where the gap is \FamExact{} points, range
$[\FamExactLo{},\FamExactHi{}]$, positive in all three. The panel is too small
for significance testing at either level --- the exact signed-rank floor at
$n\!=\!6$ is $0.031$, and no multiplicity correction clears $0.05$ (S11) --- so
we rest on effect sizes and their consistency.

\subsection{The limit is periodicity, not length}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(a) is also the paper's sharpest test. Each control has its
twin's carrier and word count, the $k$ copies of one word becoming non-adjacent
ones. Were the failure about length, attention span or exposure bias the curves
would coincide. They do not: at $k\ge6$ the median control error is \ErrCtl{}\%
$[\ErrCtlLo{},\ErrCtlHi{}]$ ($n=\ErrCtlN{}$), at every $k$ to $32$ and for every
model. The contrast is sharpest
in exactly-correct renderings, \ExactCtl{}\% for controls against
\ExactRep{}\% for their twins: decoders that miscount a repeated sequence five
times in six render its non-adjacent twin right nineteen times in twenty. Controls are not perfect --- \CtlMissPct{}\% carry genuine
truncations --- but they are exact where the repeated items are not.

Above $k\!=\!8$ the control's fillers cycle a pool of eight, making that contrast
period-$1$ against period-$8$. Re-generating $k=12\ldots32$ from a never-cycled
$146$-word pool leaves the dissociation at \ApMidGap{} points (\ApMidRep{}\%
against \ApMidCtl{}\%, $n=\ApMidN{}$) where cycled controls give \ApCycGap{}: the
confound is worth \ApCost{} points, not the bulk of it.

A third rival is a decoding rule: the families ship repetition penalties
differing by an order of magnitude, and a penalty suppresses repeated tokens by
construction. Swept on \PenNArch{} architectures (S15) the deficit stays put --- XTTS-v2 over a \PenFold{}-fold range at
\PenRepLo{}--\PenRepHi{}\% exact, Qwen3-TTS-0.6B over a \PenQFold{}-fold range at
\PenQRepLo{}--\PenQRepHi{}\% --- and with Qwen's penalty off outright it renders
\PenZeroRep{}\% against \PenZeroCtl{}\%. The \PenNoneN{} Llasa checkpoints pass
\emph{no} penalty and show the effect at full size, \PenNoneRep{}\% against
\PenNoneCtl{}\%.

The last rival is architectural, the one we cannot exclude: two
non-autoregressive systems disagree. VITS~\cite{kim2021vits} shows \emph{no}
dissociation (\VitsRep{}\% of repeated items exact against \VitsCtl{}\% of
controls, $n=90$ each at \NSeeds{} seeds, a gap of \VitsGap{} against the panel's
$+\ARPoolGap{}$), and not for want of competence: at $k\!=\!6\text{--}8$, where
the panel's gap reaches \ARMidGap{} points, it renders \NonARMidRep{}\% and
\NonARMidCtl{}\% exactly, off the floor and ordered the other way. But
F5-TTS~\cite{chen2024f5tts}, contemporary and flow-matching rather than
recurrent, \emph{does} show it: \FivettsRep{}\% against \FivettsCtl{}\%,
$+\FivettsGap{}$, growing with $k$ as the panel's does. Absence of an
autoregressive decoder confers no immunity, and we withdraw the architectural
claim.

What plausibly separates them is where the count must live: VITS gives each input
token its own duration, while F5-TTS estimates one total duration and so must
represent how much speech to make. F5-TTS lets that be tested rather than
asserted --- supply the duration a correct rendering takes, read off its own
controls --- and the answer splits: below $k\!=\!\DurSplit{}$ it lifts exact
renderings from \DurLoFree{}\% to \DurLoFixed{}\% ($n=\DurLoN{}$), at or above
it the gain is \DurHiGain{} ($n=\DurHiN{}$). Handed the right length the model
still cannot place thirty-two repetitions inside it, so the severe end of the
deficit is not a duration failure (S13). The
VITS null meanwhile does the judge's work: blank-collapse would have depressed
its repeated items too.

\subsection{The decoder buys states more slowly under repetition}

Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(ii) says states visited under periodic conditioning
stop being mutually distinguishable, so more repetitions should buy distinct
internal states more slowly than non-repetitive text of the same length. Counting
states by the trajectory's effective rank, the capacity gain on repeated text is
a factor \CapRatio{} of the control's (Figure~\ref{fig:main}(c)), positive in all
\CkCapN{} checkpoints (mean \CkCap{} $[\CkCapLo{},\CkCapHi{}]$) but varying
fourfold: general in direction, not magnitude. It is not merely the monotonous
audio a correct rendering produces (S8), and staying positive it says repetition
slows state acquisition without halting it.

Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution}'s premise holds only approximately
($\delta\le\DeltaMax{}$ nats) and its dose-response prediction fails outright:
within a $(\text{model},k)$ cell, flatter attention goes with \emph{better}
counting ($r=\DilR{}$ $[\DilRLo{},\DilRHi{}]$; S12). Whatever selects which
generations fail is not the degree of dilution.
